name: squares
about: The squares of the natural numbers from 1 to 20, punched as calculated. Manual, section 1.6, page 6, as printed.
program:
# The squares of the natural numbers from 1 to 20, punched as calculated.
# Manual, section 1.6, page 6, as printed.
1, 20 rep (j) j j × (P) ; ]

name: sum-of-squares
about: The sum of the squares of the natural numbers from 1 to 100. Manual, section 1.6, page 6. The manual leaves the sum in the accumulator; the (P) that punches it is ours.
program:
# The sum of the squares of the natural numbers from 1 to 100.
# Manual, section 1.6, page 6. The manual leaves the sum in the
# accumulator; the (P) that punches it is ours.
0, 1, 100 rep (j) j j × + ] (P) ;

name: subroutine
about: Section 1.7, page 9: read in two numbers and punch the square root of the sum of their squares, using subroutine no. 6.
program:
# Section 1.7, page 9: read in two numbers and punch the square root of
# the sum of their squares, using subroutine no. 6.
R R 6 ↓ (P) ;                       # main program
]                                   # end of main program
* 6 dup × rev dup × + .5 pow ]      # subroutine

name: polynomial
about: e = a y² + b y + c, as Hamblin's GEORGE is usually quoted. Reading a, b, c and y and punching e are ours.

name: factorials
about: a(n) = n! for all n from 1 to 15. Manual, section 1.6, page 6, as printed.
program:
# a(n) = n! for all n from 1 to 15. Manual, section 1.6, page 6, as printed.
1, 1, 15 rep (x) x × x|(a) ] ;
# Ours: punch a(1) to a(15).
1, 15 P|(a)

name: newton
about: Five iterations of x = (x + y/x)/2 from 1: "Newton's method for the square root of y". Manual, section 1.6, page 6. Setting y and punching the result are ours.

name: converge
about: Section 1.8, page 10: iterate x = (x + y/x)/2 from unity "until successive values differ by not more than e". The result is left in the accumulator. Setting y and e and punching the result are ours.

name: mean
about: Example 1, page 7: twenty numbers are read in, and their mean and root mean square computed and punched out.
program:
# Example 1, page 7: twenty numbers are read in, and their mean and root
# mean square computed and punched out.
1, 20 R|(a)                                   # read in data
0, 1, 20 rep (j) j|a + ] 20 ÷ (P) ;           # calculate and punch mean
0, 1, 20 rep (j) j|a dup × + ] 20 ÷ .5 pow (P) ;   # root mean square

name: mean-one-pass
about: Example 1, page 7, the alternative: mean and root mean square in a single repetition.
program:
# Example 1, page 7, the alternative: mean and root mean square in a
# single repetition.
1, 20 R|(a)
0, 0, 1, 20 rep (j) j|a + rev j|a dup × + rev ]
20 ÷ (P) ; 20 ÷ .5 pow (P) ;

name: nested
about: The sum of squares from 1 to n for each n from 1 to 20, stored as a(1) to a(20). Manual, section 1.6, page 7, as printed; the punching is ours.
program:
# The sum of squares from 1 to n for each n from 1 to 20, stored as
# a(1) to a(20). Manual, section 1.6, page 7, as printed; the punching is ours.
1, 20 rep (n) 0, 1 n rep (x) x x × + ] n|(a) ; ]
1, 20 P|(a)

name: matrix
about: Section 1.6, page 7: b(i) = sum over j of a(i,j) x(j), for i from 1 to n, and the quadratic form sum over i, j of a(i,j) x(i) x(j), both ways the manual gives. Reading n, the matrix and the vector, and punching, are ours.
program:
# Section 1.6, page 7: b(i) = sum over j of a(i,j) x(j), for i from 1 to n,
# and the quadratic form sum over i, j of a(i,j) x(i) x(j), both ways the
# manual gives. Reading n, the matrix and the vector, and punching, are ours.
R (n) ; 1 n 1 n R||(a) 1 n R|(x)
1 n rep (i) 0, 1 n rep (j) i j||a j|x × + ] i|(b) ; ]
1 n P|(b)
0, 1 n rep (i) 1 n rep (j) i j||a i|x j|x × × + ] ] (P) ;
0, 1 n rep (i) 0, 1 n rep (j) i j||a j|x × + ] i|x × + ] (P) ;

name: normalise
about: Section 1.7, page 9: subroutine 14 divides a pair of numbers by the square root of the sum of their squares, using subroutine 6. The main program, which gives it 3 and 4 and punches the pair, is ours.
program:
# Section 1.7, page 9: subroutine 14 divides a pair of numbers by the
# square root of the sum of their squares, using subroutine 6. The main
# program, which gives it 3 and 4 and punches the pair, is ours.
3, 4, 14 ↓ (P) ; (P) ; ]
* 14 (β) rev (α) 6 ↓ (γ) α rev ÷ β γ ÷ ]
* 6 dup × rev dup × + .5 pow ]

name: any-zero
about: Section 1.8, page 10: "If any a(j) is zero (j = 1, ... n) obey subroutine no. 3". The data, n and subroutine 3 (which punches 99) are ours.
program:
# Section 1.8, page 10: "If any a(j) is zero (j = 1, ... n) obey subroutine
# no. 3". The data, n and subroutine 3 (which punches 99) are ours.
R (n) ; 1 n R|(a)
0, 1 n rep (j) j|a 0 = ∨ ] 3 ↓
1 (P) ; ]
* 3 99 (P) ; ]

name: pairs
about: Section 1.8, page 9: "to continue indefinitely reading in pairs of numbers and punching out their sum". It ends when the cards run out, on stop 1 11-6x, "data card wanted".
program:
# Section 1.8, page 9: "to continue indefinitely reading in pairs of
# numbers and punching out their sum". It ends when the cards run out,
# on stop 1 11-6x, "data card wanted".
* 0 R R + (P) ; 0 ↑

name: simpson
about: Example 3, pages 7-8: the integral from 1 to 5 of exp(-x²/2) / (1 + exp(-a x)) dx by Simpson's rule with 16 intervals, for each of five values of a given on cards.
program:
# Example 3, pages 7-8: the integral from 1 to 5 of
#     exp(-x²/2) / (1 + exp(-a x)) dx
# by Simpson's rule with 16 intervals, for each of five values of a given
# on cards.
#
# The Simpson vector s(0) ... s(16) = 1/48, 4/48, 2/48, 4/48, ... 1/48,
# prepared by the preliminary section of program the manual gives:
1, 48 ÷ 0|(s) 16|(s) 2 × 1, 7 rep (j) j 2 ×|(s) ]
2 × 0, 7 rep (j) j 2 × 1 +|(s) ] ;
# The main part:
1, 5 R|(a)                       # read in values a1 ... a5
1, 5 rep (i) i|a (a) ;           # repeat with a = a1 ... a5 in turn
0, 0, 16 rep (j)                 # mark acc. space with zero, j from 0 to 16
j 4 ÷ 1 + (x)                    # calculate argument
dup × 2 ÷ neg exp x a × neg exp 1 + ÷   # calculate integrand
j|s × + ]                        # multiply by Simpson coefficient and add
i|(r) ; ]                        # store result; end outer repeat
1, 5 P|(r)                       # punch results

name: simpson-corrected
about: Example 3, pages 7-8, with the Simpson coefficients corrected to h/3 = 1/12, 4/12, 2/12 ... where the manual has 1/48, 4/48, 2/48 ... (erratum "simpson" in ERRATA.md). Otherwise as printed. The integral from 1 to 5 of exp(-x²/2) / (1 + exp(-a x)) dx by Simpson's rule with 16 intervals, for each of five values of a given on cards.
program:
# Example 3, pages 7-8, with the Simpson coefficients corrected to h/3 =
# 1/12, 4/12, 2/12 ... where the manual has 1/48, 4/48, 2/48 ... (erratum
# "simpson" in ERRATA.md). Otherwise as printed. The integral from 1 to 5 of
#     exp(-x²/2) / (1 + exp(-a x)) dx
# by Simpson's rule with 16 intervals, for each of five values of a given
# on cards.
#
# The Simpson vector s(0) ... s(16), prepared by the preliminary section
# of program the manual gives, with 12 for 48:
1, 12 ÷ 0|(s) 16|(s) 2 × 1, 7 rep (j) j 2 ×|(s) ]
2 × 0, 7 rep (j) j 2 × 1 +|(s) ] ;
# The main part:
1, 5 R|(a)                       # read in values a1 ... a5
1, 5 rep (i) i|a (a) ;           # repeat with a = a1 ... a5 in turn
0, 0, 16 rep (j)                 # mark acc. space with zero, j from 0 to 16
j 4 ÷ 1 + (x)                    # calculate argument
dup × 2 ÷ neg exp x a × neg exp 1 + ÷   # calculate integrand
j|s × + ]                        # multiply by Simpson coefficient and add
i|(r) ; ]                        # store result; end outer repeat
1, 5 P|(r)                       # punch results

name: tpk
about: The TPK algorithm of Knuth and Trabb Pardo, "The Early Development of Programming Languages" (STAN-CS-76-562, 1976), page 3, in ALGOL 60: read a(0) ... a(10); then for i from 10 down to 0 put y = f(a(i)), where f(t) = sqrt(|t|) + 5t^3, and write i and y, or i and "TOO LARGE" if y > 400. They give no GEORGE version. The whole program is ours, in the manual's style. The data are their example input: 1 1.5 2 2.25 2.5 2.75 3 3.25 3.5 4.5 5.5.
program:
# The TPK algorithm of Knuth and Trabb Pardo, "The Early Development of
# Programming Languages" (STAN-CS-76-562, 1976), page 3, in ALGOL 60: read
# a(0) ... a(10); then for i from 10 down to 0 put y = f(a(i)), where
# f(t) = sqrt(|t|) + 5t^3, and write i and y, or i and "TOO LARGE" if
# y > 400. They give no GEORGE version. The whole program is ours, in the
# manual's style. The data are their example input: 1 1.5 2 2.25 2.5 2.75
# 3 3.25 3.5 4.5 5.5.
#
# What GEORGE forced:
# - There is no text. "TOO LARGE" is punched as 999 (their rule, pp. 4-5).
#   Each number goes on a card of its own (section 2.3), so i and y are
#   two cards: 22 in all.
# - rep only counts up, "in unit steps, from a to b" (section 1.6, p. 6),
#   so i = 10 - j for j from 0 to 10.
# - f is subroutine 6, attached after the main program's "]" and called
#   by "6 ↓" as a monadic operator on the last cell (section 1.7, p. 8).
#   t^3 is "dup dup × ×", not "3 pow": pow goes through log, and stops on
#   1 30-21x for minus a power of two (ERRATA.md).
# - There is no "else". The if is a conditional skip to mark 8, and the
#   two ways meet at mark 9 before the "]" (section 1.8, p. 9).
# - Numbers are floating point with a 22-digit binary mantissa and are
#   punched to six figures (sections 1.2 and 2.3).
0, 10 R|(a)                         # read a(0) ... a(10)
0, 10 rep (j) 10 j - (i) (P) ;      # i from 10 down to 0: punch i
i|a 6 ↓ (y) 400 > 8 ↑               # y = f(a(i)); if y > 400 skip to mark 8
y (P) ; 9 ↑                         # punch y
* 8 999 (P) ;                       # "TOO LARGE"
* 9 ]
]                                   # end of main program
* 6 dup mod √ rev dup dup × × 5 × + ]   # subroutine 6: f(t) = √|t| + 5t³
